hints: Focus on oxidation numbers, not just atoms rearranging. Check what happens to nitrogen from start to finish.
Work out nitrogen in $\text{NO}_2$ is +4, while in $\text{HNO}_2$ it is +3 and in $\text{HNO}_3$ it is +5.
Recall the special name for when the same element is both oxidised to a higher number and reduced to a lower number in one reaction.
walkthrough:
**Assign oxidation numbers to track electrons**

Think of oxidation numbers as a book-keeping tool to see who gains and loses electrons. Let us check N, H and O in every species.

For $\text{NO}_2$: $x + 2(-2) = 0$, so $x = +4$

For $\text{HNO}_2$: $(+1) + x + 2(-2) = 0$, so $x = +3$

For $\text{HNO}_3$: $(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0$, so $x = +5$

**See what changes and what stays the same**

Hydrogen stays at +1 in both $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the acids. Oxygen stays at -2 throughout, so neither H nor O is oxidised or reduced.

$$\text{N(+4)} \rightarrow \text{N(+3) and N(+5)}$$

One N gains an electron (+4 to +3, reduction) and the other N loses an electron (+4 to +5, oxidation).

**Recognise disproportionation**

When the same element from the same starting compound is both oxidised and reduced at the same time, we call it disproportionation. That is exactly what nitrogen does here, so water is just a reactant providing H and O, not an oxidising agent.

options.A: Incorrect. Oxygen stays at -2 in $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{HNO}_2$ and $\text{HNO}_3$. Since its oxidation number does not change, it has not gained electrons.
options.B: Correct. Nitrogen starts at +4 in $\text{NO}_2$ and splits into +3 in $\text{HNO}_2$ (reduced, gains 1 electron) and +5 in $\text{HNO}_3$ (oxidised, loses 1 electron). Simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same element is disproportionation.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen is +1 in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and still +1 in both $\text{HNO}_2$ and $\text{HNO}_3$. No change means no oxidation.
options.D: Incorrect. An oxidising agent must itself be reduced by gaining electrons. Water shows no change in oxidation number for H (+1) or O (-2), so it is not oxidised or reduced here.
